pl-l2d27c12-d1e108.summary: Reports others who say virtues are good uses of natural powers, the interior ones in the mind, exterior ones being works of virtue; so they read Augustine's 'work of virtue' of exterior use and 'good use of free choice is virtue' of interior use. Virtues are good motions of the mind God makes in man, since though from free choice they exist only if God frees and helps by operating and cooperating grace, which they take as God's gratuitous will.
claims: On this view virtues are good interior motions of the mind.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e111.summary: States that they support this by testimonies of the saints.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e114.summary: Cites Augustine on John: faith is believing what you do not see; believing is a motion of the mind.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e118.summary: Cites De doctrina christiana III: I call charity a motion of the soul; if charity and faith are motions of the soul, so are virtues.
claims: Charity is a motion of the soul.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e121.summary: Reports the reply: these are to be read as 'faith is the virtue by which what is not seen is believed' and 'charity is the grace by which the soul is moved to love.'
claims: Faith and charity are the principles of motions, not the motions.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e126.summary: States that this reading is supported by what Augustine says elsewhere.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e129.summary: Cites Quaestiones Evangeliorum II: there is faith by which things not seen are believed, properly called faith.
claims: Faith is that by which one believes.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e132.summary: Cites De Trinitate XIII: the things believed are one thing, the faith by which they are believed another.
claims: Faith differs from what is believed.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e135.summary: Argues: believing differs from that by which one believes; faith is that by which one believes; so believing is not faith.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e139.summary: Adds: virtue is God's work alone; so it is not a use or act of free choice; believing is an act of free choice; so believing is not a virtue.

pl-l2d27c12-d1e142.summary: States that both sides rely on these and other reasons and testimonies, and leaves the judgment to the diligent reader.

pl-l2d27c12.summary: Reports a rival view: virtues are good uses of natural powers, the interior ones in the mind, while exterior uses are works of virtue; virtues are good motions of the mind that God makes in man, since though from free choice they exist only if God frees and helps by grace, here taken as God's gratuitous will. They cite Augustine: faith is believing what you do not see, and believing is a motion of mind; charity is a motion of the soul. Opponents read these as 'faith is the virtue by which one believes,' 'charity is the grace by which the soul is moved,' citing Augustine that faith is that by which things are believed, distinct from what is believed, so believing is not faith; and since virtue is God's work alone and believing is an act of free choice, believing is not virtue. Lombard leaves the judgment to the diligent reader.
claims: One view holds virtues are good interior motions of the mind, made by God.
On that view, grace is God's gratuitous will.
Augustine calls faith believing and charity a motion of the soul.
The opposing view reads these as the virtue by which one believes or is moved.
Faith is that by which one believes, so believing is not faith.
Virtue is God's work alone, but believing is an act of free choice.
